title: What is an Apple-1?
concept: Separate the computer, program, and replica
explanation: A CPU executes instructions, a program supplies them, and a replica is a physical implementation of a historical design. A name on a screen is not evidence of the identity of a board. This exercise labels teaching objects rather than authenticating a collection item.
challenge: Where does NEURAL1 belong, and where does the Pi belong?
answer: NEURAL1 is modern host software; the Pi is its physical host. The Apple-1 execution target in these labs is virtual.

title: A computer is not magic
concept: Trace one character through the harness
explanation: The RAM harness supplies keyboard input, lets a 6502 program store it, and records the Monitor ECHO call. The visible letter and the stored byte are two observations of the same test, not a measurement of the physical keyboard path.
challenge: What changes for an empty line, containing only Return?
answer: The buffer and screen contain a carriage return. Try echo("\r") and compare the instruction count.

title: Your first hex number
concept: Convert bytes between decimal and hexadecimal
explanation: One hexadecimal digit represents four bits. Two digits represent a byte. Divide by 16: the quotient is the high digit and the remainder is the low digit. 42 = 2 times 16 + 10, so 42 is $2A.
challenge: Convert 200 before running Python to check it.
answer: 200 = 12*16+8, so $C8. A byte cannot contain 256; that needs a larger representation.

title: Facts, models, and evidence
concept: Distinguish an observation from a claim
explanation: A checksum, an emulator result, and a physical observation answer different questions. This fixture exercises labels; the labels themselves are a worked reasoning example. Explain why an observed virtual result cannot establish a live board result.
challenge: Does a passing checksum authenticate an original Apple-1?
answer: No. It identifies matching bytes; provenance and physical authentication require different evidence.

title: The 6502 at work
concept: Follow fetch, decode, execute
explanation: LDA immediate loads a value into A; STA copies A into memory; JMP chooses the next instruction address. The trace records state before each instruction. Read the next row, or the final registers, to see the effect.
challenge: Replace $2A with $10. Predict memory and the program byte that changes.
answer: The immediate operand changes from 2A to 10, and $0400 contains $10 (16).

title: Memory is a map
concept: Addresses name locations; bytes hold values
explanation: A 16-bit address identifies one of 65,536 locations. The same byte can be data or an opcode depending on how it is used. These virtual locations are inside the declared lab RAM window; this is not the physical Replica memory map.
challenge: What address follows $03FF?
answer: $0400. Carry crosses the low byte; it is not $040A.

title: Binary, bits, and bytes
concept: Use masks to inspect bits
explanation: A mask selects bits. AND with $7F clears bit 7 while preserving the other seven bits; OR with $80 sets it. This is arithmetic on a byte, independent of whether the byte represents a character.
challenge: What does XOR $80 do if applied twice?
answer: It toggles bit 7 each time, so applying it twice restores the original byte.

title: Characters become numbers
concept: Decode high-bit keyboard characters
explanation: The repository harness explicitly sets bit 7 on input and masks it for screen text. That convention must not be confused with ordinary seven-bit ASCII. Carriage return is $0D in ASCII and $8D with the high bit set.
challenge: Decode C1 A0 C2 8D.
answer: A, space, B, carriage return: "A B\r".

title: Instructions change state
concept: Initialize arithmetic state explicitly
explanation: ADC includes carry. CLD selects binary arithmetic and CLC clears carry before an addition. Relying on a simulator default makes a program harder to explain or move. The two runs below differ only in the explicit carry setup.
challenge: Why does CLC alone not establish binary arithmetic on an unknown machine state?
answer: The decimal flag is separate; use CLD when the program requires binary ADC behavior.

title: Meet the Monitor
concept: Use the three Monitor operations
explanation: The modeled Monitor can inspect, deposit, and run. It is a tiny machine interface, not a host shell or an assembler. Here the exact byte string is deposited in virtual memory before the run command is accepted.
challenge: Will LOAD PROGRAM work in this modeled Monitor?
answer: No. Assembly and host shell commands are not Monitor commands.

title: Addresses and byte entry
concept: Explain origin and little-endian operands
explanation: An absolute address occupies two operand bytes, low byte first. STA $0400 becomes 8D 00 04. The origin determines where instruction bytes live; it does not change the destination of that absolute store.
challenge: What bytes encode the address $1234?
answer: 34 12, low byte then high byte.

title: A safe rehearsal loop
concept: Predict an echo before running it
explanation: The line-input harness feeds HI followed by carriage return. It records the screen, the stored buffer, instruction count, and the return path. A matching test supports this program in this harness; it does not establish serial or electrical behavior.
challenge: Try A + Return and compare against HI + Return.
answer: One fewer ordinary character reduces the work. Record the actual count rather than assuming a timing measurement.

title: Debugging as observation
concept: Compare expectation with observation
explanation: An expected value is useful only if it was written before observing the result. A mismatch is a reason to investigate both the code and the expectation. This deliberate mistake is detected by a numeric comparison rather than hidden.
challenge: What single change could test whether the immediate operand caused the mismatch?
answer: Change only #$2B to #$2A, preserve the first result, and compare the rerun.

title: Why `JMP $FF1F` matters
concept: Separate a warm-entry jump from a subroutine return
explanation: A JMP transfers control directly. RTS expects a return address placed on the stack by a compatible call. These examples entered at the lab origin, so no caller return address is promised. A deliberate JMP $FF1F gives this virtual harness a defined exit.
challenge: Why is RTS appropriate after JSR ECHO but not an automatic substitute for the final JMP?
answer: JSR creates a return address for that call; the program entry path need not have done so.

title: Read an instruction
concept: Read mnemonic, addressing mode, and operand
explanation: The # character means an immediate value. Without it, LDA $0400 loads the byte stored at that address. The assembler turns the instruction into bytes; neither mnemonic text nor a label is sent directly to the CPU.
challenge: Why is STA #$41 invalid?
answer: STA needs a destination address; an immediate literal is a value, not a writable destination.

title: Variables in memory
concept: Store and retrieve a variable
explanation: A variable label is a source-code name for storage. The CPU uses numeric addresses. After storing $5A at $0402, loading from that address into X must produce the same value unless intervening code changes it.
challenge: If the program occupies $0300-$0319, why is $0310 a poor buffer?
answer: It overlaps instruction bytes. An input store could change a future instruction.

title: Counting and looping
concept: Compare zero and sign loop conditions
explanation: DEX changes X and the zero and negative flags. BNE repeats until zero. BPL repeats while bit 7 is clear, which includes zero. Starting at five, the BPL version therefore decrements once more and finishes at $FF.
challenge: What happens if the BNE countdown starts at zero?
answer: The first DEX wraps to $FF; it takes 256 decrements to reach zero again.

title: Decisions and branches
concept: Test both sides of a branch
explanation: CMP sets flags without replacing A. BEQ takes the equal case; the other path must not fall through into it accidentally. These two runs exercise the same decision with matching and nonmatching inputs.
challenge: Would testing only Y reveal a broken non-Y path?
answer: No. Include a matching key, a nonmatching key, and boundary or malformed inputs when relevant.

title: Keyboard to screen
concept: Follow input, buffer storage, echo, and return
explanation: The existing RAM program waits for a ready key, reads it, stores it at the indexed buffer position, echoes it, compares against carriage return, and either continues or exits. Empty input is a separate test: Return itself is still a character.
challenge: Why does the saved buffer include carriage return?
answer: The store happens before the carriage-return comparison and exit.

title: Design a tiny utility
concept: Build a fill utility from a testable design
explanation: Define the count and the allowed destination range before writing instructions. This routine fills exactly five bytes with A and exits. Checking the byte just after the range catches an extra iteration.
challenge: Make a copy utility instead. What additional cases should its design card include?
answer: Zero length, maximum length, overlapping source/destination, and preserving the source when required.

title: From instructions to BASIC
concept: Compare language levels without inventing a BASIC runtime
explanation: A BASIC expression delegates arithmetic and output to an interpreter. Assembly exposes the storage and instructions. This host calculation checks the arithmetic idea only: the repository does not bundle a runnable Apple-1 BASIC interpreter for this exercise.
challenge: Does storing the answer 42 implement multiplication?
answer: No. It demonstrates representing one result; a general multiply routine or interpreter performs the operation.

title: Variables, input, and output
concept: Separate input, state, computation, and output
explanation: A small program has a data path. Here the input is an integer and the output is twice it. This Python host analogue illustrates the flow; it does not validate Apple-1 BASIC syntax or string allocation rules.
challenge: What would you specify before accepting negative or fractional input?
answer: The numeric domain, conversion rules, errors, and representation. Apple-1 Integer BASIC is not interchangeable with Python numeric behavior.

title: Algorithms: recipes for information
concept: Turn an ambiguous algorithm into explicit operations
explanation: An algorithm states how the next step is chosen and when work stops. The host trace below replaces "add the numbers" with initialize, read one item, update, and stop at the end of the finite list.
challenge: What result should the algorithm produce for an empty list?
answer: Zero if the sum specification defines an empty sum as zero; write that rule explicitly.

title: Sorting by hand
concept: Trace sorting instead of trusting the final list
explanation: Adjacent comparisons and swaps can sort a list. A pass with no swaps supplies a stopping condition. Save intermediate lists so a correct final result does not conceal a different algorithm or an incorrect comparison count.
challenge: Why retain the final no-swap pass?
answer: It is the evidence used by this version of the algorithm to stop; it still performs comparisons.

title: Data, files, and the CF card
concept: Separate a source artifact, a record, and a backup
explanation: A filename extension does not establish a role or execution authority. A content hash can show that a copied byte sequence matches. It does not establish that a file is suitable for a card layout or a physical launcher.
challenge: Does committing a .hex file make it CF-card approved?
answer: No. Manifest approval, layout validation, and physical deployment are separate steps.

title: Pictures made of letters
concept: Design within a 40-column text grid
explanation: ASCII art is a layout problem with a fixed character budget. Count characters rather than judging the width by eye. These lines use only uppercase seven-bit printable characters and spaces.
challenge: Add your own title without changing the border width.
answer: The interior is 38 characters; reject or shorten longer text before centering.

title: Motion is many pictures
concept: Model animation as frames and state
explanation: An animation can be described by position and direction. These host-generated frames show state updates, not display timing or cursor addressing on the Apple-1. A time delay and a display update mechanism would be additional implementation work.
challenge: What state is needed for a bouncing symbol beyond its position?
answer: Its direction, and the boundaries of its allowed movement.

title: Generative patterns
concept: Generate a pattern from a compact rule
explanation: A rule can describe many rows more compactly than storing every character. This triangular pattern has a simple row counter. Compact description is not evidence of learning, emergence, or randomness.
challenge: How many stars occur in the first six rows?
answer: 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21. Compare a stored image with the size and runtime cost of a generator.

title: Interactive fiction
concept: Represent a story as explicit state transitions
explanation: A room is state; an action selects a transition. An unavailable exit must have defined behavior. This host example makes invalid movement stay in the current room instead of accidentally selecting another one.
challenge: Where would you store whether a key has been collected?
answer: In separate persistent game state; the current room alone cannot represent inventory.

title: Sound, rhythm, and code
concept: Encode a rhythm without claiming audio hardware
explanation: Bits can encode events over equal conceptual time slots. A one means a clap and zero a rest. The same bits do not specify tempo, duration, volume, pitch, or a sound device.
challenge: What extra parameter turns the slots into a tempo?
answer: A defined time per slot. Generating sound also needs a compatible output mechanism.

title: The 1976 personal-computing moment
concept: Order source-backed events without merging different counts
explanation: This exercise sorts an intentionally shuffled teaching timeline. The dates are drawn from the existing lesson source notes. Sorting them checks ordering logic; it is not independent verification of the underlying historical sources.
challenge: Why should "boards made" and "boards sold" be separate timeline facts?
answer: They count different events. One number cannot replace the other without evidence.

title: Original, replica, and reproduction
concept: Use object labels as bounded claims
explanation: The teaching labels below distinguish an original artifact, a modern replica, and a digital model. A label does not authenticate an actual object; it states the category whose evidence would need checking.
challenge: Can a software model reproduce behavior without being a physical replica?
answer: Yes. Behavioral correspondence and physical object identity are different questions.

title: Why provenance matters
concept: Check identity with a cryptographic digest
explanation: SHA-256 detects a change to the bytes being hashed. It supplies a content identity, not the creator, date, license, or historical authenticity of that content. Compare the original and a changed copy.
challenge: What fields would you add to turn a digest into a useful provenance record?
answer: Source, acquisition date, original filename, version, responsible person, rights information, and the claim the file supports.

title: Safe experimentation
concept: Classify the action before touching the machine
explanation: An off-device computation and a serial open have different effects. This is a worked classification exercise, not an authorization engine. A classroom label cannot approve a hardware procedure.
challenge: Why is a no-transmit serial open not automatically harmless here?
answer: The project recorded display corruption after such an open. Its physical evidence gate remains relevant.

title: The future history you are making
concept: Keep observations separate from interpretations
explanation: A useful log records the action, observed result, and interpretation as different fields. This authored sample is a record-format exercise; it does not assert that a new physical observation occurred.
challenge: Where should you record a surprising result that contradicts your expectation?
answer: In observation, with the actual output retained. Put the hypothesis explaining it in interpretation.

title: The monitor that wasn't
concept: Preserve unknowns in a collection claim
explanation: A later display can be associated with a historical computer without being its original bundled display. This exercise intentionally leaves a claim unknown instead of filling the gap from an attractive photograph.
challenge: Would a modern museum pairing establish a 1976 factory bundle?
answer: No. It establishes a display choice in that later context. Check the lesson sources and image provenance.

title: Hex scavenger hunt
concept: Decode a known byte artifact without calling it a live dump
explanation: The address column is computed from the stated origin. The bytes are read from the repository file, not memory on the Replica. Decode instructions using opcode boundaries rather than treating every occurrence of a byte as an opcode.
challenge: Why can the byte D0 mean something other than BNE in this listing?
answer: It can be an operand byte, such as the high byte of address $D010. Instruction boundaries determine interpretation.

title: Fix the loop
concept: Expose a one-byte off-by-one error
explanation: The intended destination is five bytes long. The broken comparison uses six, so both programs return normally but one writes beyond the intended region. A successful return alone cannot detect this defect.
challenge: Which operand byte changes, and why is that a better fix than changing the stated intention?
answer: The immediate comparison operand changes from 06 to 05. It makes the implementation meet the original five-byte specification.

title: Build a museum demo
concept: Design a demonstration that works without the board
explanation: Choose one visible result, explain it, and ask the viewer a question. The timing below is a rehearsal plan. Code verifies the budget, not whether an audience learned the concept.
challenge: What should you ask the audience after presenting?
answer: Ask them to explain the one result in their own words. A timed script is not evidence of comprehension.

title: Curate a mini software exhibit
concept: Curate a set with explicit evidence limits
explanation: A useful exhibit connects an artifact, what it shows, and what it cannot prove. This exercise checks that every sample card states a limit; historical authenticity and rights still require source review.
challenge: What strengthens the exhibit more: a confident caption or a precise source record?
answer: A precise source record lets a reviewer evaluate the caption. Confidence supplies no additional evidence.

title: Invent the next lesson
concept: Write an observable learning objective
explanation: "Understand assembly" does not specify how learning is checked. An objective should name a task, visible output, and criterion. A completed author card is a proposal requiring review, not a new approved curriculum item.
challenge: How would you assess an open-ended program design?
answer: Use a rubric covering requirements, memory ranges, reachable exit, tests including boundaries, source notes, and an honest limit statement.

title: Two Boards, One Computer
concept: Compare implementations without confusing the software contract
explanation: The existing atlas compares documented functions, not verified probe points. The mapping below is a reading exercise derived from that atlas. A similar address interface does not imply identical circuitry or timing.
challenge: Which substitutions would a program using the documented I/O addresses need to know about?
answer: The program depends on the software-visible contract; circuitry, electrical behavior, and timing still matter for physical compatibility.

title: Validate console commands before work starts
concept: Validate console commands before work starts
explanation: The parser validates syntax before the application checks storage or launches a worker. A suggested correction is advice, not an automatically executed command. This lab exercises the real parser without a deployment configuration.
challenge: Why must START extra be rejected rather than ignored?
answer: The extra argument may express an assumption about what will run. Ignoring it can start unintended work.

title: Assemble source and retain its execution trace
concept: Assemble source and retain its execution trace
explanation: The lesson assembler performs two passes so a branch can refer to a later label. This is host-side teaching tooling. The constrained experimental agent does not receive this assembler API as an extra tool.
challenge: Can you infer physical clock timing from the trace instruction count?
answer: No. The bounded software trace is not an electrical or cycle-accurate Replica measurement.

title: Record a provider response and replay its exact identity
concept: Record a provider response and replay its exact identity
explanation: A recording binds a response to its prompt, agent, and seed. Exact replay must refuse a missing tuple rather than supply a plausible replacement. The provider below is deliberately fake, so this tests recording behavior without inference.
challenge: Would fixing only the random seed reproduce a different model build?
answer: No. Preserve weights/manifest identity, configuration, prompt, runtime, and recordings. A seed is only one input.

title: Qualify a test model registry without downloading weights
concept: Qualify a test model registry without downloading weights
explanation: A registry identifies the backend, exact model, context bound, settings, and provenance. Qualification checks a bounded provider configuration. This fake record is marked TEST-ONLY; its qualification is not native Ollama model acceptance.
challenge: What must replace placeholder metadata before a real campaign?
answer: Locally observed model identities, digests, quantization, context/settings, license, and provenance information.

title: Cancel and resume without duplicating committed turns
concept: Cancel and resume without duplicating committed turns
explanation: A checkpoint is useful when an interrupted run resumes with its earlier transcript intact. The synthetic provider requests cancellation after its first call. Resume uses the actual campaign engine and the same specification, without a systemd worker or a live model.
challenge: What would invalidate a same-ID resume?
answer: Changing the canonical specification or losing the original effective model registry undermines the meaning of continuing the same run.

title: Verify an export and detect changed evidence
concept: Verify an export and detect changed evidence
explanation: Export creates a separate evidence package with a file manifest. Verification detects content changes. A correct hash does not prove that a scientific interpretation is correct, but a changed hash can invalidate a claim of unchanged evidence.
challenge: Why keep the original export when experimenting with tampering?
answer: It preserves a reference. This lab changes only its own temporary fixture, never retained research evidence.

title: Persist claims, history, and review thresholds
concept: Persist claims, history, and review thresholds
explanation: META stores statements and evidence relationships. A tribunal verdict depends on declared rules and evidence level, not the confidence of a model explanation. This synthetic claim is a database exercise, not a new scientific result.
challenge: Would an authored causal_level=2 make this fixture a causal discovery?
answer: No. It exercises the rules; the evidence itself is explicitly synthetic.

title: Evaluate 4k-mind with explicit controls
concept: Evaluate 4k-mind with explicit controls
explanation: Persistent RAM can survive a context boundary, but that does not by itself show learned culture. This fixture executes a known output routine and asks the real family evaluator to inspect it independently.
challenge: What negative control would prevent an always-pass evaluator from appearing correct?
answer: Use an empty/incorrect program or a structurally invalid candidate and require rejection. A positive fixture alone is insufficient.

title: Evaluate selfhost1 with explicit controls
concept: Evaluate selfhost1 with explicit controls
explanation: A successful raw-code task is stage-one evidence. It is not the discovery of an assembler or compiler. This fixture supplies a known routine and checks the implemented family criterion.
challenge: What negative control would prevent an always-pass evaluator from appearing correct?
answer: Use an empty/incorrect program or a structurally invalid candidate and require rejection. A positive fixture alone is insufficient.

title: Evaluate 256-byte-universe with explicit controls
concept: Evaluate 256-byte-universe with explicit controls
explanation: An exact-size candidate must be explicitly deposited and perform its task. Padding an eight-byte routine to a declared 256-byte artifact is a positive test fixture, not a complete replacement Monitor.
challenge: What negative control would prevent an always-pass evaluator from appearing correct?
answer: Use an empty/incorrect program or a structurally invalid candidate and require rejection. A positive fixture alone is insufficient.

title: Evaluate ram-republic with explicit controls
concept: Evaluate ram-republic with explicit controls
explanation: Two scheduled participants can interact through shared RAM. This fixture repeats an authored routine for both participants; it checks the evaluator, not the emergence of a protocol.
challenge: What negative control would prevent an always-pass evaluator from appearing correct?
answer: Use an empty/incorrect program or a structurally invalid candidate and require rejection. A positive fixture alone is insufficient.

title: Reject unsupported historical proposals
concept: Reject unsupported historical proposals
explanation: Historical validation cannot manufacture missing components or prices. This negative example asks the actual family evaluator to inspect an empty proposal set. It should evaluate the input while declining to call it a valid design.
challenge: Does the reviewed year-end corpus promote the broad March-1976 staging index?
answer: No. The two datasets have different source and cutoff scopes.

title: Ground Field Library operations in a real lesson corpus
concept: Ground Field Library operations in a real lesson corpus
explanation: SOURCE reads the selected lesson documents without inference. ASK/HINT/EXPLAIN/CHECK assemble bounded, source-grounded prompts; TRACE first executes a deterministic program. A fixed provider here exposes that plumbing without claiming model understanding.
challenge: Does a source-grounded prompt guarantee that a real model answer is true?
answer: No. Inspect citations and deterministic evidence, test abstention, and keep model explanation separate from execution.

title: Restore a snapshot and identify a one-factor fork
concept: Restore a snapshot and identify a one-factor fork
explanation: A snapshot captures state; a manifest identifies scientific inputs. A fork names its parent and changed factor. Restoration is a host verifier operation, not a hidden memory tool given to the agent.
challenge: Why preserve the same seed when changing one factor?
answer: It helps define a matched comparison, but does not eliminate every confound or guarantee identical model execution.

title: Reset private context while retaining shared RAM
concept: Reset private context while retaining shared RAM
explanation: The scheduler owns agent contexts, while the world owns memory. Resetting an agent conversation must not silently erase persistent RAM. Conversely, sharing model weights must not share private conversation lists.
challenge: Would persistence of an authored byte demonstrate a learned communication protocol?
answer: No. It demonstrates state behavior. A protocol claim needs operational criteria, controls, and replication.

title: Inspect recorded native evidence without rerunning the Pi
concept: Inspect recorded native evidence without rerunning the Pi
explanation: This reads the published sanitized September closeout extract. It is a retained native observation, not fresh inference or a new hardware health check. The source record separates the model response, parser acceptance, and independent execution.
challenge: Can reading this file establish that the Pi is healthy now?
answer: No. It establishes what the retained record reports about that identified run.

title: Inspect a synthetic disk image without touching a disk
concept: Inspect a synthetic disk image without touching a disk
explanation: The storage inspector accepts an ordinary image file. Here a tiny teaching image contains an MBR signature and one partition entry. It is not a bootable Pi image or a storage device.
challenge: Would a valid MBR signature prove all files in the image are intact?
answer: No. It validates one structure, not the complete filesystem or historical provenance.

title: Separate portal navigation from a physical launcher
concept: Separate portal navigation from a physical launcher
explanation: The portal is a virtual state machine. Selecting COMPUTER changes its state and calls a virtual adapter. It neither opens a device nor resolves the physical launcher integration.
challenge: Does selecting COMPUTER in this example run a real Woz Monitor ROM?
answer: No. The adapter reports a modeled interface; the physical launcher remains separate.

title: Validate a 40-column frame and preserve artwork rights
concept: Validate a 40-column frame and preserve artwork rights
explanation: Visual formatting has executable constraints, while permission to redistribute an image is a separate provenance question. Validate the original text portal without treating an external reference as a licensed project asset.
challenge: Why is fitting a 40-column frame unrelated to redistribution permission?
answer: One checks formatting; the other depends on authorship, rights, and permission records.

title: Read display modes without executing deployment controls
concept: Read display modes without executing deployment controls
explanation: The same recorded data can have human-readable or JSON presentation. Long IDs must remain copyable. This exercises the actual presentation function and the resource-bounded preset definitions; it does not launch a worker.
challenge: Why should the display preserve a negative passed field?
answer: Readable presentation must not turn completed execution into a claim of success.

title: Inspect a local-provider request using a mock transport
concept: Inspect a local-provider request using a mock transport
explanation: The real Ollama adapter constructs a request to a loopback endpoint. The injected opener below checks that request and supplies a synthetic reply. This is a transport contract demonstration; it does not contact Ollama or infer tokens.
challenge: How would a real request differ?
answer: It would use an existing qualified local model and the actual service, with resource checks, bounded generation, and retained recordings.

title: Check a preserved program source without writing a card
concept: Check a preserved program source without writing a card
explanation: The host-side CF flow begins with a source manifest and explicit approval. A source file hash can be inspected independently of export or deployment. This example reads only the existing RAM artifact and card manifest.
challenge: What is the next safe step after reviewing a manifest?
answer: Host-side staging of approved sources, following the exporter guide. Staging is not physical-card deployment.

title: Rebuild a synthetic SELFHOST archive artifact
concept: Rebuild a synthetic SELFHOST archive artifact
explanation: The persistent archive retains reconstruction evidence and ancestry. This deliberately synthetic stage-one run deposits a known routine. The archive ingests it, rebuilds it, and verifies a dependency-closed export; it does not invent a compiler.
challenge: What is additionally required before later-stage qualification?
answer: Qualified parent ancestry, a retained builder, exact repeat reconstruction, independently declared behavioral tests, and controls. Stage one alone supplies none of those later claims.

title: Copy and verify a migration using disposable fixture directories
concept: Copy and verify a migration using disposable fixture directories
explanation: The storage workflow separates planning, copying, and verification. This example creates its own marked temporary directories and tiny fixture file. It does not identify a real SSD, change mounts, format a device, or finalize deletion of user data.
challenge: Why not finalize deletion as the first teaching step?
answer: Verification and an independent retained copy come first. Finalization is a separately guarded operator action, not a requirement for learning copy integrity.

title: Observe a deployment guard refusing an ordinary directory
concept: Observe a deployment guard refusing an ordinary directory
explanation: A directory with a familiar name is not necessarily the commissioned volume. This example invokes the actual storage verification guard with a freshly created ordinary directory. Rejection is the expected success of the guard.
challenge: Why check a filesystem identity rather than only free space?
answer: A missing mount can leave an ordinary directory on another disk. Plenty of free space on the wrong disk does not make the destination correct.

title: Inspect research staging without promoting it
concept: Inspect research staging without promoting it
explanation: The historical research index carries an explicit status and authoritative-record count. Reading or validating that file does not promote its claims. This capture reflects the committed staging index, separate from the reviewed console corpus.
challenge: What would justify promotion of a historical component?
answer: The documented source, hash, claim, date-cutoff, and review gates; model-generated estimates are not a substitute.

title: Read token accounting without confusing words and tokens
concept: Read token accounting without confusing words and tokens
explanation: Tokens belong to a model tokenizer, not the Apple-1 byte encoding. The mock API reports token counters; the adapter retains them rather than counting words. The numbers below are explicitly supplied fixture metadata, not measured inference.
challenge: Can you infer token count from the number of ASCII bytes?
answer: No. The tokenizer determines segmentation. Preserve the provider-reported counters and model identity.

title: Estimate weight storage without promising total RAM use
concept: Estimate weight storage without promising total RAM use
explanation: Parameter count multiplied by nominal bits per weight gives a lower-level storage estimate. It excludes metadata, quantization scales, runtime allocations, and context/KV cache. It is not a memory-fit benchmark or a model recommendation.
challenge: Why can a nominal 750 MB weight estimate exceed 750 MB in actual memory?
answer: Scales and metadata, activation/runtime buffers, allocator overhead, and the context cache all add storage.

title: Separate model context from persistent machine memory
concept: Separate model context from persistent machine memory
explanation: A conversation context and a byte in virtual RAM are different stores. This lab clears an authored Python context list while preserving a world snapshot. A later real-model experiment would need to show what the model can recover from RAM through its permitted interface.
challenge: Does the retained byte guarantee the next model will interpret it correctly?
answer: No. The model still needs a usable convention and must discover or follow it through the allowed observations.

title: Treat a model response as a proposal, not an instruction to the host
concept: Treat a model response as a proposal, not an instruction to the host
explanation: The response parser selects permitted modeled Monitor command lines. Assembly, shell instructions, and explanations do not become host actions merely because a model prints them. Acceptance also does not guarantee the resulting program is correct.
challenge: What if valid-looking commands store the wrong value?
answer: The parser has checked syntax only. Independent execution and the task evaluator must check behavior.

title: Distinguish model names from content identity
concept: Distinguish model names from content identity
explanation: A friendly tag can name different content over time. A manifest digest and a GGUF weight digest identify different artifacts. This authored metadata example teaches which identity each field describes; it does not qualify a real model.
challenge: Which digest should you substitute for a missing license?
answer: Neither. Content identity and permission/provenance are different registry fields.

title: Interpret latency from a retained native run
concept: Interpret latency from a retained native run
explanation: Elapsed campaign time and model request latency are not interchangeable with tokens per second. This reads a retained native run and reports only its recorded elapsed time and accepted-command count. It performs no new benchmark.
challenge: Why not divide eight commands by elapsed time and call it model tokens per second?
answer: Commands and tokens are different units, and elapsed time includes additional work. Use the relevant provider counters and durations.

title: Bound a research matrix before launching it
concept: Bound a research matrix before launching it
explanation: Cartesian products multiply quickly: models times experiments times seeds, with additional generations and agents inside each cell. A bounded plan makes the cost and stopping criteria explicit before inference.
challenge: Why is a per-cell deadline different from an overall resource guarantee?
answer: Concurrency, runtime overhead, cache state, thermal behavior, and external failures still need explicit supervision.

title: Use negative controls before widening a claim
concept: Use negative controls before widening a claim
explanation: A useful evaluator must distinguish a candidate that meets the task from one that does not. This lesson uses the exact-256 evaluator with a positive and a negative authored fixture, so "the evaluator ran" cannot substitute for "the task passed."
challenge: Does passing a positive control establish a general replacement Monitor?
answer: No. It establishes that specific output/return task under its explicit constraints.

title: Use deterministic mutation and selection policies
concept: Use deterministic mutation and selection policies
explanation: Mutation, selection, conflict accounting, and convergence are explicit policies. The seed makes an authored mutation repeatable; a shared artifact does not establish a causal explanation for convergence.
challenge: Would changing the score weights change what counts as the best candidate?
answer: Yes. Declare the weights before inspecting candidates and retain them as part of the experiment.

title: Inspect a llama.cpp command without executing a binary
concept: Inspect a llama.cpp command without executing a binary
explanation: The real adapter uses an argument array and bounded runner. An injected runner records the invocation and supplies a fixture response; there is no model binary or GGUF file opened in this lab.
challenge: Why use an argument array rather than concatenate a shell command?
answer: It preserves argument boundaries and avoids interpreting model or path text as shell syntax.

title: Stage only approved CF sources in a disposable directory
concept: Stage only approved CF sources in a disposable directory
explanation: The actual exporter reads explicit approval fields. This fixture has one approved source and one candidate. It checks that staging copies the approved page and leaves the candidate out, without writing a card.
challenge: Does this promote any real lesson to card-approved status?
answer: No. The approval fields and sources in this lab are disposable fixtures.

title: Audit candidate firmware source without loading firmware
concept: Audit candidate firmware source without loading firmware
explanation: The static auditor inspects archived source declarations. Its result is explicitly candidate-only. Source pin constants and writer routines do not identify installed EEPROM contents, safe probe points, or the actual cause of a hardware fault.
challenge: What evidence would connect this source to the installed firmware?
answer: A separately verified identity and readback/provenance procedure; static source inspection alone cannot do so.

title: Reject incomplete capture metadata
concept: Reject incomplete capture metadata
explanation: A capture needs enough context to support interpretation. The validator should reject an incomplete object even when its result says PASS. This lab creates no physical capture and verifies no probe placement.
challenge: Is a complete metadata object sufficient to establish that a measurement happened?
answer: No. Raw artifacts, identities, hashes, procedure, and interpretation still matter.

title: Package only explicitly selected support evidence
concept: Package only explicitly selected support evidence
explanation: The support-bundle tool copies explicit files into an archive with hashes. The teaching file is created in a disposable directory. No workstation logs, account data, serial devices, or private machine configuration are collected.
challenge: Why should a support bundle require explicit paths?
answer: It limits collection scope and makes it possible to review exactly what is included before sharing.

title: Interpret invariant mining as a candidate generator
concept: Interpret invariant mining as a candidate generator
explanation: A feature common to observed successes is a candidate pattern, not an automatically established cause. An independent successful counterexample can break it. Keep outcome classification and the population used in analysis explicit.
challenge: What would justify changing an observed pattern into a causal claim?
answer: A predeclared intervention/control design, appropriate uncertainty analysis, and replication, not a detector label alone.

title: Link a proof capsule to explicit falsification work
concept: Link a proof capsule to explicit falsification work
explanation: A proof capsule packages the basis for a claim and its reproduction metadata. A falsification plan proposes an intervention. Neither creates a scientific finding simply because its data structure is valid.
challenge: Why leave a compute estimate unbenchmarked?
answer: An unmeasured cost should remain unknown rather than be presented as a measured performance result.

title: Exercise the single-writer contract model
concept: Exercise the single-writer contract model
explanation: This FIFO is a host model of a proposed firmware contract, not installed firmware. Two producers enqueue bytes and one service path preserves their order. Overflow must stop rather than silently drop data.
challenge: What additional work would be needed before claiming this fixes a physical fault?
answer: Qualified source identity, review, bounded instrumented procedures, actual measurements, and recovery evidence. This model supplies none of those physical observations.

title: Connect a virtual echo program to a fixed-response bridge
concept: Connect a virtual echo program to a fixed-response bridge
explanation: The off-device bridge first executes the RAM input program, then formats a supplied response for a 40-column display. A fixed client separates bridge plumbing from real-model inference.
challenge: Which part changes when substituting a real local model?
answer: The provider call and its provenance/resource requirements. The deterministic echo and formatting contracts remain independently testable.

title: Values and addresses
concept: Distinguish immediate, zero-page and absolute loads
explanation: The # marker makes $20 a value. Without it, the CPU reads a location. A load can change A and N/Z without changing memory. The example stores three results so the distinction stays visible. Zero-page scratch here is for the CPU lab, not an experiment-agent privilege.
challenge: Change LDA #$20 to LDA $20 before the first store. Is that byte initialized yet?
answer: No. This program writes $20 later. In this zero-initialized world the first result becomes zero, but an arbitrary physical machine need not start with zero there.

title: Copy a table with sentinels
concept: Follow an indexed copy from source bytes to a destination range
explanation: DATA names the actual address after the final JMP. LDA DATA,Y reads source+Y; STA $0400,Y writes destination+Y. The loop executes for Y=0..4. Sentinels at $03FF and $0405 catch writes immediately outside the five-byte destination. The forward-label regression check ensures the assembler sizes the load correctly.
challenge: Change CPY #$05 to CPY #$06. Predict the first failing check.
answer: A sixth source byte is read and $0405 is overwritten, so the upper sentinel check fails. A clean Monitor return is insufficient.

title: Carry and signed overflow
concept: Read C, Z, N and V as different questions
explanation: Binary ADC computes A+operand+incoming carry. C reports an unsigned ninth bit. V reports a signed result outside -128..127. N reflects result bit 7 and Z a zero byte. $7F+1 has V=1 and C=0; $FF+1 has C=1 and V=0. CLD fixes the arithmetic mode before every test.
challenge: Predict $40+$40 with CLC: result, C and V.
answer: Result $80, C=0, V=1. Unsigned 64+64 fits a byte; signed +128 does not fit signed eight-bit range.

title: Carry a result across two bytes
concept: Implement a 16-bit little-endian addition
explanation: Add the low bytes with CLC once. Store the low result, load the high operand, and ADC the high operand while preserving carry. LDA and STA preserve C, even though LDA changes N/Z. The memory pair $00,$01 is $0100, or 256.
challenge: Insert CLC immediately before the second ADC. What is lost?
answer: The carry from $FF+1 disappears; the high result becomes $00, incorrectly giving $0000 instead of $0100.

title: Subtract and compare deliberately
concept: Use carry as no borrow and separate signed comparison
explanation: SBC computes A-operand-(1-C), so ordinary subtraction begins with SEC. CMP leaves A intact and sets flags as a comparison; carry set means unsigned A>=operand. N alone is not a general signed-less-than test when signed overflow is possible.
challenge: Why does starting 5-3 with CLC give 1?
answer: CLC supplies an incoming borrow: 5-3-(1-0)=1. With SEC it is 5-3-(1-1)=2.

title: Masks, shifts and rotates
concept: Track selected bits and carry through a rotate
explanation: AND clears selected bits, ORA sets selected bits, and EOR flips selected bits. ASL shifts bit 7 into C and shifts zero into bit 0. ROL includes carry as a ninth bit in the operation; the following STA does not destroy that carry.
challenge: Insert CLC before ROL A. Predict the last stored byte.
answer: The last byte becomes $04 instead of $05 because the incoming bit is zero.

title: Calls and the page-one stack
concept: Balance JSR/RTS and PHA/PLA while preserving A
explanation: The caller loads A with $41 and calls SUB. JSR stores two return bytes; the stack pointer goes from $FF to $FD. PHA saves A and moves SP to $FC. PLA restores A and RTS consumes the call frame. The subroutine writes Z at $0401 but preserves A for the caller to store A at $0400. These traces show Py65 state, not electrical stack cycles.
challenge: Remove PLA. Can RTS still find its matching return frame?
answer: No. The saved accumulator is above the return bytes, so RTS pulls the wrong pair. The final memory/exit/SP checks expose the unbalanced stack.

title: Two kinds of indexed pointers
concept: Separate indexing a pointer from indexing its destination
explanation: A zero-page pointer occupies a low byte followed by a high byte. ($20),Y reads that pointer then adds Y; ($20,X) adds X within zero page before reading a pointer. The first example deliberately crosses $04FF to $0500. These are NMOS CPU forms, and their allowed use still depends on the surrounding experiment policy.
challenge: Set Y=0 in the first indirect load. Does it still read $0500?
answer: No. The pointer is $04FF, so without the increment it reads $04FF, which this fixture leaves zero.

title: Labels and branch arithmetic
concept: Calculate a relative branch and reject an unreachable target
explanation: The displacement is target-(branch address+2), encoded as a signed byte. -3 becomes $FD. Branches reach -128..127 from the following PC. The lesson assembler now rejects a far target instead of silently wrapping it and resolves forward data labels after instruction sizes stabilize.
challenge: A branch begins at $0300 and targets $0381. Is it in range?
answer: Yes. $0381-$0302=$7F, or +127. $0382 would be out of range.

title: Review the original A06 program
concept: Execute the exact thirteen-byte answer and its zero-length pitfall
explanation: This is the original A06 countdown fill, not the five-byte fill in its older companion. Starting Y=$0F performs 16 stores and leaves Y=$FF. Encoding a supposed zero length as Y=$FF still enters the body once, writes $04FF, decrements to $FE and exits because N is set. A count parameter needs an explicit zero test and a clearly stated supported range.
challenge: Does this DEY/BPL loop support every length from 1 to 256?
answer: No. Its signed continuation test gives a restricted range and surprising behavior for high initial indices. Design a different loop with a zero precheck when a full byte count is required.

title: Derive the keyboard boundary
concept: Test empty input and both sides of the 128-character exit
explanation: For n<=127 ordinary characters, setup contributes 1 instruction, each ordinary pass contributes 10, the CR pass contributes 8, and the final JMP contributes 1. Thus 10*(n+1). With 128 ordinary characters, Y reaches $80 before the supplied CR is read, giving 1282 instructions and a buffer with no CR. The harness reads a maximum 128 buffer bytes.
challenge: What happens for 127 ordinary characters followed by Return?
answer: It stores and echoes 128 bytes including the CR, returns to Monitor, and uses 1280 instructions. This differs from 128 ordinary characters followed by Return.

title: Reset, BRK and interrupt return
concept: Distinguish vectors and actual CPU BRK from a lab stop marker
explanation: This example steps Py65 directly with an explicit reset vector, IRQ/BRK vector and RTI handler. BRK saves a return PC of BRK+2 plus status, and RTI restores it. The repository world deliberately stops before executing BRK, so its BRK stop report does not demonstrate an interrupt handler. This is a software semantic check, not a hardware reset or IRQ measurement.
challenge: Can a world result with stop_reason BRK prove an interrupt handler executed?
answer: No. That world intercepts BRK before the CPU instruction runs. Use the direct CPU exercise to study the instruction and identify the different evidence mode.

title: Inspect fresh local-model evidence
concept: Re-evaluate actual generated proposals and compare controls
explanation: The retained workstation runs used identified cached Qwen weights and Ollama 0.33.2 through both generate and chat APIs. Each arithmetic control returned 4, while the four bounded 6502 proposals failed the declared task. This lab verifies hashes and independently re-executes retained proposal text; it requests no new inference. An authored positive and boundary-violating negative check the same evaluator. Passing the lab confirms reproduction of the recorded finding, not a successful model-generated program. The Pi record adds actual Phi-4 inference on an identified Raspberry Pi 5; its two proposals also fail this strict task. This is not a comparison benchmark because model, runtime and host differ.
challenge: Does four failed proposals prove that Qwen cannot write any 6502 program?
answer: No. They describe these two prompts, seed, weights, runtime and output/context bounds. They are not a benchmark, and neither the arithmetic control nor an authored positive control establishes general model competence.

title: Read the installed Pi tutor and trace
concept: Separate generated tutoring from deterministic native execution
explanation: The retained console calls ran on the commissioned Pi and its pinned September application. HINT and EXPLAIN supplied useful statements; CHECK abstained and ASK incorrectly declined an available fact. TRACE retained actual program bytes and a three-instruction Monitor return. This lab verifies those records and independently executes the recorded bytes on the host. The runtime grounded flag describes its support path; it does not certify factual accuracy. A follow-up with the revised source on the real Pi correctly enumerates all three Monitor functions. This lab verifies that record and exactly replays its retained provider response against the current source excerpt, without inference. This is a staged-source observation; the installed global release remains pinned.
challenge: Can grounded=True prove that the ASK response is correct?
answer: No. This recorded ASK response abstains despite the lesson containing the three functions. Compare the source, the generated text and deterministic evidence; do not substitute a metadata flag for review.

title: A real Integer BASIC greeting
concept: Run INPUT and DIM on the preserved interpreter
explanation: A string must be dimensioned before INPUT. This session runs the identified Apple-1 interpreter on a modeled NMOS 6502; its echo, automatic question mark and greeting are interpreter output.
challenge: Put a question mark at the end of the prompt. What changes?
answer: The prompt supplies one question mark and INPUT supplies another. The exact NAME?? behavior is covered by the BASIC boundary tests.

title: Integer conversion with a checked domain
concept: Prevent intermediate arithmetic overflow
explanation: Integer division truncates. Multiplication happens before division here: 129*254 fits, but 130*254 exceeds 32767. The program checks 0 through 129 before computing.
challenge: Try 0, 129, 130 and -1. Which inputs reach the calculation?
answer: 0 and 129 yield 0 and 327 cm. 130 and -1 print the domain message. Fractional input is outside this integer-only program contract.

title: A running sum in BASIC
concept: Trace a loop and its accumulated state
explanation: FOR, NEXT and integer storage are executed by the original interpreter. The printed running totals expose each update instead of checking only the final answer.
challenge: Change the bound from 5 to 6. Predict the last two numbers.
answer: The final index is 6 and the accumulated sum is 21. State the intended behavior before changing the bound to zero.

title: Bubble sort in real Apple-1 BASIC
concept: Compare each pass with the B04 paper trace
explanation: The real interpreter executes adjacent comparisons and swaps. Integer arrays are one-based: DIM A(5) permits indices 1 through 5; index 0 raises RANGE ERR. The final no-swap pass is retained.
challenge: Try the already sorted and reverse-sorted starting orders from B04.
answer: Already sorted: 4 comparisons, 0 swaps. Reverse order: 20 comparisons, 10 swaps, including the final no-swap pass.

title: A BASIC quiz with both outcomes
concept: Exercise a conditional and a nonmatching answer
explanation: The interpreter reads an integer and selects a response. A successful answer alone would not validate the other branch, so the tests exercise a wrong answer too.
challenge: Answer 41, then rerun and answer 42.
answer: 41 prints the hint 2*16+10; 42 prints CORRECT: 42. Both reach END and return to the BASIC prompt.

title: Generate a triangular pattern in BASIC
concept: Produce text from nested loop state
explanation: A row loop chooses the length and a column loop prints that many stars. PRINT with a semicolon stays on the line; a bare PRINT ends it. The interpreter emits all characters.
challenge: How many stars are generated, and how many loop rows?
answer: Six rows and 21 stars. This is a deterministic generator, not randomness or learning.

title: Compile every lesson for a 40x24 screen
concept: Check all card pages and RAM bounds
explanation: The compiler includes all 42 original packet readings, activities, text worksheets and answers. Model, feature, CPU, native-evidence and new lab guides provide host routes. The uppercase reading copy is explicitly separate from exact host commands.
challenge: Why can a valid Markdown file still fail this card build?
answer: Display dimensions, unsupported characters, book size, filename and reader memory limits are additional constraints. A Markdown file is not a CFFA1 launcher.

title: Let real CFFA1 firmware build a virtual file
concept: Inspect a ProDOS file independently after firmware writes it
explanation: The preserved CFFA1 ROM runs on an NMOS 6502 with modeled ATA registers. It formats only a new in-memory test card, writes a file and reads it back. A separate Python ProDOS reader checks the result.
challenge: Does this prove the installed CFFA1 or physical card works?
answer: No. It checks this identified firmware against the declared ATA model. Installed identity, bus behavior, timing and physical media remain hardware acceptance work.

title: Navigate the RAM card reader
concept: Run actual pager instructions and verify visible text
explanation: The RAM reader uses the real CFFA1 API and a modeled keyboard/display. The rehearsal checks first page, next, previous, answer jump, book selection and Monitor exit. These are CPU results, not physical screen photographs.
challenge: What happens if the reader is launched with the wrong prefix?
answer: It shows a CFFA error and offers another book selection. Choose EDUCATION in the CFFA menu before loading the reader.

title: Save and restore BASIC in CFFA1 format
concept: Generate a real BA1 file and execute the restored program
explanation: The interpreter tokenizes the authored program. CFFA1 SaveBASICFile emits its A1 header and $F1 file; LoadBASICFile restores state into cleared RAM. A BASIC warm start then executes the restored program.
challenge: Why would renaming a .bas text file to a BASIC filename be insufficient?
answer: CFFA1 BA1 stores interpreter state and tokenized memory, including a versioned header. Plain source text is a different format. Use the interpreter and save API rather than a filename trick.
